screens.title: Identity-based Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Identity-based policies are the standard way to give permissions to IAM users, groups, and roles. They declare what an identity can do, such as read objects from S3 or call specific A P I actions. A clear example is attaching AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess to a role used by an auditing account; that role can then list and read buckets when assumed. Identity policies are evaluated when a principal makes a request, but they do not stand alone: resource-based policies and organization SCPs can further restrict what actions are actually permitted. A common misconception is to assume that giving an identity a permission always allows access regardless of resource settings; in reality both identity-based and resource-based policies must allow the action, and SCPs can still cap permissions. Practical significance: attach permissions to roles rather than long-lived users when possible, and scope permissions with condition keys like aws:SourceIp or aws:RequestedRegion to reduce risk. Check your policies with the IAM policy simulator before deploying. Question: when would you prefer a role with a narrow permission set over a long-lived user with the same permissions? Identity-based Policies means attach permissions to identities to declare allowed actions; always test with the simulator and prefer roles to long-lived users.. In practical terms, policies attached to users, groups, and roles that define allowed actions for that identity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Identity-based Policies
Definition
Attached to users, groups, and roles; declare what the identity can do.
  • Grant actions (Allow) or explicitly deny actions.
  • Can include condition keys to restrict by IP, time, or request context.
  • Prefer to attach to roles for services and delegation, not long-lived users.
Common mistake
Assuming identity policies alone decide access. Resource policies or SCPs can still block the action.
Key Takeaway
Identity policies state what an identity may do; they should be narrow, tested, and applied to roles where possible.
Concrete Example
A central auditing role has AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess attached. When an auditor assumes this role, that identity inherits the permission to list and read objects.
Illustrative policy (JSON)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetObject"],
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket", "arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/*"]
    }
  ]
}
Misconception
Giving a role S3 permissions guarantees access even if the bucket denies it. Resource policies can still deny the action.
Pro tip
Use condition keys to scope access, for example require requests from a trusted IP range or specific VPC endpoint.

screens.title: Resource-based Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Resource-based policies attach to resources like S3 buckets, SQS queues, or KMS keys and explicitly list which principals can access that specific resource and what actions they may perform. For example, an S3 bucket policy can permit a principal from a different AWS account to GetObject; this is how you allow cross-account reads without giving the principal identity-based permissions in the bucket account. Importantly, allowing access in a resource policy does not override identity policies—the request is evaluated against both. A common pitfall is granting overly broad resource policies that allow 'Everyone' or allow external accounts by mistake. Use Access Analyzer to detect when a policy grants access to external entities. In practice, prefer explicit ARNs in resource policies and consider conditions such as aws:PrincipalOrgID to restrict access to principals within your organization. Real-world benefit: resource policies enable precise, resource-scoped sharing without creating duplicate identities in each account. Resource-based Policies means resource policies declare who may use the resource; they work in concert with identity policies and should be narrowly scoped and validated.. In practical terms, policies attached directly to resources to specify which principals can access them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Resource-based Policies
Definition & Behavior
Attached to a resource; specifies which principals and what actions are allowed on that resource.
  • Common on S3 buckets, SQS queues, and KMS keys.
  • Can grant cross-account access without creating identities in the resource account.
  • Still subject to identity policies and SCPs during evaluation.
Common mistake
Using wildcard principals or "Everyone" grants unintended public access. Always prefer specific ARNs or organization-based restrictions.
Why this helps
Resource policies enable precise resource sharing across accounts and services without distributing identity credentials.
Concrete Example: S3 bucket policy
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_B_ID:root"},
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"],
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::my-cross-account-data-a-12345", "arn:aws:s3:::my-cross-account-data-a-12345/*"]
    }
  ]
}
Note: combine this with a narrow identity policy in the trusting account. Use Access Analyzer to detect if the policy allows external principals unintentionally.
Check your policy
When you grant cross-account access, verify the principal ARN, resource ARNs, and any conditions such as aws:PrincipalOrgID to keep access within your organization.

screens.title: Service Control Policies (SCPs)
screens.narratorSegment: Service Control Policies are part of AWS Organizations and act as top-level guardrails. SCPs do not grant permissions; instead they filter the maximum allowed actions across accounts in an OU. If an SCP denies an action, no identity-based or resource-based policy within that account can override it. This makes SCPs ideal for enforcing compliance rules, such as preventing any account in Production from using a disallowed service or blocking public S3 bucket ACLs. A practical example is denying s3:DeleteBucket across a Production OU to prevent accidental deletion. A common misconception is thinking SCPs provide fine-grained per-role controls; rather, they are broad caps and should be used sparingly and tested before applying. Use the policy simulator and test accounts to confirm outcomes before wide deployment. Final reflection: use SCPs to define what is never allowed in an account, and rely on identity and resource policies to manage daily permissions within that cap. Service Control Policies (SCPs) means scps restrict the maximum permissions available in accounts; they are enforcement guardrails, not permission grants.. In practical terms, organization-level guardrails that set maximum permissions for accounts and ous. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: SCPs restrict the maximum permissions available in accounts; they are enforcement guardrails, not permission grants.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Service Control Policies
What SCPs do
SCPs limit the maximum set of permissions available to all principals in an account. They cannot grant permissions but can deny actions globally.
  • Attach at the root, OU, or account level.
  • Use to enforce organization-wide security and compliance guardrails.
  • Test carefully: denies can unintentionally block automation.
Common use cases
Prevent certain services in Production, deny public S3 ACLs, or block region-specific resource creation across an OU.
Concrete Example
An SCP that denies s3:DeleteBucket for all accounts in a Production OU prevents accidental deletion even if an identity has delete permissions locally.
Misconception
SCPs do not replace least-privilege identity design. They are caps, not a substitute for testing and narrow permissions.
Pro tip
Use a deny list sparingly and validate effects in staging accounts before applying to Production OUs.

screens.title: How Policy Evaluation Works
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding policy evaluation is crucial to diagnosing access failures. When a request is made, AWS first considers organization-level controls such as Service Control Policies to see if the action is allowed at the account boundary. If an SCP denies the action, evaluation ends in denial. If not denied by an SCP, AWS evaluates identity-based policies attached to the calling principal and any resource-based policies attached to the target resource. For access to be allowed, it must be explicitly allowed by both the identity policy and the resource policy, and not explicitly denied by any applicable policy. A common mistake is assuming that an allow in one policy is sufficient; in many cross-account scenarios an S3 bucket policy must also allow the principal. Troubleshooting tip: check the effective policy statement in the IAM policy simulator and then use Access Analyzer for resource-based checks. Consider this question: if an identity has explicit allow but the resource policy lacks the matching allow, will the request succeed? The correct answer is no. This layered evaluation ensures the strictest applicable constraints win and helps you design safer multi-account permissions.

keyIdea.title: Evaluation rule
keyIdea.text: SCPs cap permissions; both identity and resource policies must allow an action and no explicit deny can exist for access to succeed.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Policy Evaluation
Evaluation Steps
01
SCP check
If an SCP denies the action, the request is denied regardless of other policies.
02
Identity policy evaluation
Identity-based policies attached to the principal are evaluated for allow or deny.
03
Resource policy evaluation
Resource-based policies are checked; the action must be allowed here as well.
04
Final decision
Allow only if allowed and not explicitly denied by any applicable policy.
Troubleshooting tip
Use the policy simulator to step through decisions and run Access Analyzer for resource policies to find external principals.
Concrete Contrast
If a user has s3:ListBucket allowed but the bucket policy does not allow that user or denies it, the request will fail. This contrast helps explain common access denied errors in cross-account setups.
Reflection question
When you see Access Denied, start by checking for explicit denies in SCPs and resource policies before modifying identity policies.
Key Takeaway
The most restrictive applicable policy wins; SCPs cap, identity and resource policies must both allow.

screens.title: Cross-Account Access with IAM Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Cross-account access via IAM roles is a secure delegation pattern that avoids creating duplicate users or sharing long-lived credentials. The trusted account creates a role with a permission policy that grants the actions needed on its resources. Its trust policy then specifies which principals from the trusting account may assume the role. The trusting account grants its user or role permission to call sts:AssumeRole for that role. When assumed, the principal receives temporary security credentials scoped to the role's permissions. A concrete example: a 'CrossAccountS3ReadOnlyRole' in Account A grants List and Get on a bucket, and Account B's principal is allowed to assume it. This pattern reduces credential sprawl and centralizes permissions where resources live. A common misconception is that assume-role copies the user's original permissions into the trusted account; it does not—the principal gains only the permissions defined in the role's permission policy. Always record and rotate trust relationships and consider adding MFA requirement for sensitive operations. How would you audit which accounts can assume a given role? Use the trust policy and Access Analyzer to review external trusts.

keyIdea.title: Cross-account pattern
keyIdea.text: Use roles with trust policies for secure delegation; the assumed role grants only the role's permissions and yields temporary credentials.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Cross-Account Roles
Pattern Overview
Trusted account defines a role with a permission policy and a trust policy. Trusting account principals assume that role via sts:AssumeRole and receive temporary credentials.
Trusted Account
Creates role, attaches permission policy, sets trust policy to allow Account B's principals.
Trusting Account
Gives its user or role permission to call sts:AssumeRole on the role ARN in Account A.
  • Temporary credentials have a limited duration and reduce long-lived key risk.
  • Trust policies can include conditions, e.g., MFA or source account constraints.
  • Audit trust relationships and use Access Analyzer to identify external trusts.
Key takeaway
Roles are the secure mechanism for cross-account delegation; they issue temporary credentials scoped to the role policy.
Concrete Example: Trust Policy
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_B_ID:root"},
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}
This trust policy allows principals from Account B to assume the role. Pair it with a narrow permission policy in the trusted account to limit actions available during the session.
Misconception
Assuming a role does not merge the caller's original permissions with the role's; the session only receives the role's permission policy.

screens.title: Assume-Role CLI Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough shows how to assume a role from the trusting account and use the temporary credentials returned to access resources in the trusted account. First, configure the AWS CLI with the trusting account user's access key and secret. Then call sts assume-role with the role ARN from the trusted account and a session name. The response contains temporary AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and SessionToken. Export those as environment variables in your shell to make subsequent CLI calls use the temporary session. For example, after exporting the credentials, running aws s3 ls will list buckets accessible under the assumed role. A common pitfall is forgetting to export the session token, which causes requests to fail. Another is assuming the role has the same permissions as your original user; the session is limited to the role's permission policy. After testing, always unset the temporary environment variables. This pattern demonstrates the power of temporary credentials: they provide time-bound access and reduce the risk of long-lived credential leakage. In practical terms, hands-on commands to assume a role and use temporary credentials to list s3 buckets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Assume-Role CLI
Step-by-step
1) Configure CLI profile for the trusting account user. 2) Call sts assume-role with the trusted role ARN. 3) Export returned temporary credentials. 4) Run resource commands; then unset credentials when finished.
Common mistake
Not exporting the session token or leaving temporary credentials set in a shared shell after the lab.
Key takeaway
Temporary credentials are powerful for delegation but must be handled carefully and revoked by unsetting environment variables after use.
Commands (illustrative)
# Configure profile for trusting account user
aws configure --profile cross-account-user

# Assume the role in Account A
aws sts assume-role \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_A_ID:role/CrossAccountS3ReadOnlyRole \
  --role-session-name S3CrossAccountSession \
  --profile cross-account-user

# Export temporary credentials (example values)
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=""
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=""
export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=""

# List buckets using temporary credentials
aws s3 ls

# Unset when done
unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
Replace placeholders with actual values returned by assume-role. If you see Access Denied, verify role permissions and that you exported the session token.

screens.title: IAM Access Analyzer
screens.narratorSegment: IAM Access Analyzer inspects resource-based policies and role trust policies to find when resources are shared with external entities. It flags buckets, KMS keys, SQS queues, and roles that allow access to principals outside your account or organization. For example, if an S3 bucket policy inadvertently grants GetObject to everyone, Access Analyzer will create a finding showing the external access path, the affected resource, and the offending statement. A common misconception is treating Access Analyzer as enforcement; it is an analysis and alerting tool that helps you detect issues but does not by itself block access. Use its findings to remove broad principals, add organization-based conditions, or tighten principals to specific ARNs. Operationally, schedule regular reviews of findings and integrate them into your audit pipeline so that new exposures are caught early. Final question: after Access Analyzer flags a bucket with external access, what are three corrective actions you might take? Consider removing public principals, adding a PrincipalOrgID condition, or tightening resource ARNs. IAM Access Analyzer means access analyzer finds cross-account and public access in resource and trust policies so you can remediate unintended exposures.. In practical terms, identify resources shared with external principals and surface unintended access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › IAM Access Analyzer
What it does
Analyzes resource-based and trust policies to detect when a resource is shared with an external principal or is publicly accessible.
  • Creates findings with the resource ARN, offending statement, and suggested remediation steps.
  • Detects external account principals and public access patterns.
  • Integrate findings into your regular audits and automation pipelines.
Misconception
It warns you about exposure; it does not automatically change policies. You must remediate findings or automate fixes separately.
Why review findings
Regular review prevents accidental data leaks and enforces least privilege across resources and accounts.
Example finding
"S3 bucket my-cross-account-data-a-12345 allows GetObject to principal arn:aws:iam::111222333444:root" — Access Analyzer explains the statement and suggests narrowing the principal or adding organization conditions.
Remediation options
Remove public principal entries, replace root or wildcard ARNs with specific role ARNs, or add aws:PrincipalOrgID to restrict to your organization.

screens.title: Temporary Security Credentials
screens.narratorSegment: Temporary security credentials are short-lived credentials issued when a role is assumed. They are preferred because they narrow the window of exposure compared to long-lived access keys embedded in code or configuration. Services like EC2, Lambda, and ECS assume roles to obtain temporary credentials automatically, and human users can obtain temporary credentials via IAM Identity Center or sts:AssumeRole. A concrete example: when you assume CrossAccountS3ReadOnlyRole, the returned credentials expire after the session duration, limiting an attacker’s ability to reuse stolen keys. A common misbelief is that rotating long-lived keys frequently is equivalent to temporary credentials; while rotation reduces risk, temporary sessions provide automatic expiration and are less likely to be leaked in code. Operationally, avoid embedding access keys in repositories, use Secrets Manager for necessary keys, and enforce role-based access for services. Question: what immediate benefit do temporary credentials provide when combined with limited role permissions? They cut both the scope and the lifetime of any compromise. Temporary Security Credentials means short lifespan plus scoped permissions reduce blast radius and the utility of stolen credentials.. In practical terms, why temporary credentials are preferred over long-lived access keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Temporary Credentials
Why prefer temporary credentials
They automatically expire, limit exposure if leaked, and are issued with the permissions defined by the assumed role.
  • Automatically used by AWS services when a role is attached to compute instances.
  • Reduce the need to store or rotate long-lived access keys in code.
  • Combine with narrow role policies for minimal privilege sessions.
Practical rule
Prefer role-based temporary credentials for automation and service accounts; use Secrets Manager only when long-lived keys are unavoidable.
Concrete Scenario
A CI/CD pipeline assumes a role to deploy artifacts. The role's temporary credentials expire after the job completes, preventing reuse if logs leak credentials. If the pipeline used a static access key, compromise could persist until rotation.
Misconception
Frequent rotation of long-lived keys equals temporary sessions. Rotation helps but doesn't remove the operational risk of storing keys in code.
Best practice
Use roles for compute and human sessions, and ensure logs and scripts never print secrets to shared places.

screens.title: Policy Design & Validation
screens.narratorSegment: Designing secure IAM policies requires deliberate scoping and validation. Use condition keys to narrow the context of an allow, for example restrict actions by source IP, required MFA, or aws:PrincipalOrgID so the right callers at the right times can act. Always validate candidate policies with the IAM policy simulator to simulate A P I calls from a principal and see the effective decision. After deployment, run Access Analyzer to detect if resource-based or trust policies expose resources externally. One practical workflow: author a narrow policy, simulate expected actions, deploy to a staging account, run Access Analyzer, and then gradually roll out to production. A common error is authoring broad allow statements with wildcard resources. Prefer explicit ARNs or resource tags to limit permissions. Also follow operational rules: avoid embedding keys in code, rotate secrets when necessary, and document role trusts. End with this reflection: which condition keys are most helpful in your environment to reduce risk while enabling necessary access? Policy Design & Validation means use condition keys and simulation to create narrow, testable policies; then validate with access analyzer after deployment.. In practical terms, use condition keys, the policy simulator, and access analyzer to design safe policies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Policy Design & Validation
Design rules
Limit actions and resources, prefer role-based delegation, and apply condition keys such as aws:SourceIp, aws:PrincipalOrgID, or aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent where appropriate.
  • Use explicit resource ARNs instead of wildcards where possible.
  • Require MFA for sensitive console actions via conditions.
  • Tag resources and use tag conditions to scope access by environment.
Validation workflow
Author → Simulate in policy simulator → Deploy to staging → Run Access Analyzer → Roll out to Production.
Common pitfall
Applying broad permissions with wildcards and then relying on SCPs to catch mistakes. SCPs are safety nets but not replacements for least-privilege design.
Concrete Example: Condition Key
{
  "Sid": "AllowFromOrg",
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/*",
  "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-1234567890"}}
}
This condition limits access to principals under the specified organization ID, preventing external accounts from using the policy.
Pro tip
Combine tag-based conditions and PrincipalOrgID to scope access by environment and organization boundaries.

screens.title: Policy Types Compared
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right policy type depends on scope and control intent. Identity-based policies are for granting actions to specific users, groups, or roles—use them when you control the principal and want to assign permissions to identities. Resource-based policies live on the resource and are ideal for sharing with external accounts without creating identities in the resource account; they explicitly state which principals may access the resource. Service Control Policies are organization-level caps that prevent certain actions across accounts; use them for broad compliance and security guardrails such as banning a service in Production. A practical contrast: to allow a central audit role to read buckets, attach an identity-based permission to the role and add a resource policy granting that principal access. To prevent any account from making buckets public, apply an SCP deny at the OU level. A frequent error is misusing SCPs for day-to-day permissions—they are blunt instruments and can block automation if misapplied. Closing question: for a single resource shared with one external account, which policy type should you prefer and why? The resource policy is best because it provides explicit resource-scoped sharing without creating cross-account identities.

keyIdea.title: Comparison summary
keyIdea.text: Identity policies for principals, resource policies for resource-scoped sharing, SCPs for organization-wide caps—combine them thoughtfully.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Policy Types Compared
Identity-based policies
Attach to users, groups, and roles. Use to grant permissions to known principals and prefer roles for services and delegation.
Resource-based policies
Attach to resources to allow specific principals or accounts to access that resource. Ideal for cross-account sharing without duplicating identities.
Service Control Policies
Organization-level caps that prevent actions across accounts; they do not grant permissions and should be used as guardrails.
When to choose
Identity: internal principals. Resource: sharing with external accounts. SCP: enforce organization-wide limits.
Misuse warning
Avoid over-relying on SCPs to correct broad identity or resource policy mistakes; fix the root policy design.
Takeaway
Combine policy types intentionally: SCPs for caps, identity/resource policies for operational access.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are three concise ideas to carry forward. First, identity-based policies attach to principals and declare what those identities may do; test them with the policy simulator and prefer role attachments over long-lived users. Second, resource-based policies live on the resource and are the right tool for cross-account sharing—always scope principals and use conditions like PrincipalOrgID where appropriate. Third, Service Control Policies provide organization-level guardrails by limiting the maximum permissions in accounts; they do not grant permissions and must be used sparingly and tested carefully. Keep in mind the policy evaluation rule: an action is allowed only if SCPs permit it and both identity and resource policies allow it without explicit deny. Use Access Analyzer to find unintended external sharing and rely on temporary credentials to reduce the lifetime and impact of credential compromise.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we advance from basic IAM to the controls and patterns you need for secure multi-account AWS environments. You will learn the three policy layers—identity-based, resource-based, and Service Control Policies—and how they combine to determine effective permissions. We'll explore secure cross-account access with IAM roles and walk through a CLI-based example that produces temporary credentials. You will also see how IAM Access Analyzer helps detect resources unintentionally shared outside your boundaries and why temporary credentials reduce long-term risk compared to embedded access keys. Finally, we'll cover policy design practices such as using condition keys, validating with the policy simulator, and applying the principle of least privilege. This matters because in a multi-account organization small misconfigurations can become widespread risks; guardrails like SCPs and short-lived role sessions help you enforce consistent security policies while keeping operations flexible. As you progress, pay attention to how each mechanism complements the others and consider one quick question: where would you apply an SCP versus a resource policy in your environment?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish identity-based, resource-based, and organization-level Service Control Policies, and understand how they combine to produce effective permissions. You will implement a cross-account access pattern using IAM roles, obtaining temporary credentials and avoiding shared long-lived keys. You will interpret IAM Access Analyzer findings and take corrective action for resources that are shared unintentionally. You will also apply policy design best practices: use condition keys to narrow scope, validate policies with the IAM policy simulator and Access Analyzer, and favor least privilege. Each objective pairs a clear skill with why it matters: separating who can act from what a resource allows reduces surprises; roles enable secure delegation without credential sharing; automated analysis finds hidden exposures early; and temporary credentials and validation reduce the chance of persistent compromise. These are practical skills you can use in real multi-account AWS organizations to improve security posture while keeping operations manageable.

This second objectives slide focuses on validation and practical skills. You will practice creating a cross-account role and using the AWS CLI to assume it, observing how temporary credentials are issued and used. You will verify that both identity-based and resource-based policies must allow an action, and learn to read evaluation outcomes where an explicit deny or an SCP blocks an action. You will run the IAM policy simulator to test a policy before deployment and consult Access Analyzer to find resources shared outside your intended boundaries. Beyond technical steps, you will learn common checks: avoid long-lived keys in code, require role assumption for service accounts, and set least-privilege permission boundaries. These validation skills matter because they turn abstract rules into repeatable tests, letting you automate safety checks and prevent configuration drift across multiple accounts.

Identity-based policies are the standard way to give permissions to IAM users, groups, and roles. They declare what an identity can do, such as read objects from S3 or call specific A P I actions. A clear example is attaching AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess to a role used by an auditing account; that role can then list and read buckets when assumed. Identity policies are evaluated when a principal makes a request, but they do not stand alone: resource-based policies and organization SCPs can further restrict what actions are actually permitted. A common misconception is to assume that giving an identity a permission always allows access regardless of resource settings; in reality both identity-based and resource-based policies must allow the action, and SCPs can still cap permissions. Practical significance: attach permissions to roles rather than long-lived users when possible, and scope permissions with condition keys like aws:SourceIp or aws:RequestedRegion to reduce risk. Check your policies with the IAM policy simulator before deploying. Question: when would you prefer a role with a narrow permission set over a long-lived user with the same permissions? Identity-based Policies means attach permissions to identities to declare allowed actions; always test with the simulator and prefer roles to long-lived users.. In practical terms, policies attached to users, groups, and roles that define allowed actions for that identity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Resource-based policies attach to resources like S3 buckets, SQS queues, or KMS keys and explicitly list which principals can access that specific resource and what actions they may perform. For example, an S3 bucket policy can permit a principal from a different AWS account to GetObject; this is how you allow cross-account reads without giving the principal identity-based permissions in the bucket account. Importantly, allowing access in a resource policy does not override identity policies—the request is evaluated against both. A common pitfall is granting overly broad resource policies that allow 'Everyone' or allow external accounts by mistake. Use Access Analyzer to detect when a policy grants access to external entities. In practice, prefer explicit ARNs in resource policies and consider conditions such as aws:PrincipalOrgID to restrict access to principals within your organization. Real-world benefit: resource policies enable precise, resource-scoped sharing without creating duplicate identities in each account. Resource-based Policies means resource policies declare who may use the resource; they work in concert with identity policies and should be narrowly scoped and validated.. In practical terms, policies attached directly to resources to specify which principals can access them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Service Control Policies are part of AWS Organizations and act as top-level guardrails. SCPs do not grant permissions; instead they filter the maximum allowed actions across accounts in an OU. If an SCP denies an action, no identity-based or resource-based policy within that account can override it. This makes SCPs ideal for enforcing compliance rules, such as preventing any account in Production from using a disallowed service or blocking public S3 bucket ACLs. A practical example is denying s3:DeleteBucket across a Production OU to prevent accidental deletion. A common misconception is thinking SCPs provide fine-grained per-role controls; rather, they are broad caps and should be used sparingly and tested before applying. Use the policy simulator and test accounts to confirm outcomes before wide deployment. Final reflection: use SCPs to define what is never allowed in an account, and rely on identity and resource policies to manage daily permissions within that cap. Service Control Policies (SCPs) means scps restrict the maximum permissions available in accounts; they are enforcement guardrails, not permission grants.. In practical terms, organization-level guardrails that set maximum permissions for accounts and ous. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding policy evaluation is crucial to diagnosing access failures. When a request is made, AWS first considers organization-level controls such as Service Control Policies to see if the action is allowed at the account boundary. If an SCP denies the action, evaluation ends in denial. If not denied by an SCP, AWS evaluates identity-based policies attached to the calling principal and any resource-based policies attached to the target resource. For access to be allowed, it must be explicitly allowed by both the identity policy and the resource policy, and not explicitly denied by any applicable policy. A common mistake is assuming that an allow in one policy is sufficient; in many cross-account scenarios an S3 bucket policy must also allow the principal. Troubleshooting tip: check the effective policy statement in the IAM policy simulator and then use Access Analyzer for resource-based checks. Consider this question: if an identity has explicit allow but the resource policy lacks the matching allow, will the request succeed? The correct answer is no. This layered evaluation ensures the strictest applicable constraints win and helps you design safer multi-account permissions.

Cross-account access via IAM roles is a secure delegation pattern that avoids creating duplicate users or sharing long-lived credentials. The trusted account creates a role with a permission policy that grants the actions needed on its resources. Its trust policy then specifies which principals from the trusting account may assume the role. The trusting account grants its user or role permission to call sts:AssumeRole for that role. When assumed, the principal receives temporary security credentials scoped to the role's permissions. A concrete example: a 'CrossAccountS3ReadOnlyRole' in Account A grants List and Get on a bucket, and Account B's principal is allowed to assume it. This pattern reduces credential sprawl and centralizes permissions where resources live. A common misconception is that assume-role copies the user's original permissions into the trusted account; it does not—the principal gains only the permissions defined in the role's permission policy. Always record and rotate trust relationships and consider adding MFA requirement for sensitive operations. How would you audit which accounts can assume a given role? Use the trust policy and Access Analyzer to review external trusts.

This walkthrough shows how to assume a role from the trusting account and use the temporary credentials returned to access resources in the trusted account. First, configure the AWS CLI with the trusting account user's access key and secret. Then call sts assume-role with the role ARN from the trusted account and a session name. The response contains temporary AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and SessionToken. Export those as environment variables in your shell to make subsequent CLI calls use the temporary session. For example, after exporting the credentials, running aws s3 ls will list buckets accessible under the assumed role. A common pitfall is forgetting to export the session token, which causes requests to fail. Another is assuming the role has the same permissions as your original user; the session is limited to the role's permission policy. After testing, always unset the temporary environment variables. This pattern demonstrates the power of temporary credentials: they provide time-bound access and reduce the risk of long-lived credential leakage. Assume-Role CLI Walkthrough means use sts assume-role to receive temporary credentials, export them to the environment, then run commands as the assumed role; remember to unset after testing.. In practical terms, hands-on commands to assume a role and use temporary credentials to list s3 buckets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

IAM Access Analyzer inspects resource-based policies and role trust policies to find when resources are shared with external entities. It flags buckets, KMS keys, SQS queues, and roles that allow access to principals outside your account or organization. Choosing the right policy type depends on scope and control intent. Identity-based policies are for granting actions to specific users, groups, or roles—use them when you control the principal and want to assign permissions to identities. Resource-based policies live on the resource and are ideal for sharing with external accounts without creating identities in the resource account; they explicitly state which principals may access the resource. Service Control Policies are organization-level caps that prevent certain actions across accounts; use them for broad compliance and security guardrails such as banning a service in Production. A practical contrast: to allow a central audit role to read buckets, attach an identity-based permission to the role and add a resource policy granting that principal access. To prevent any account from making buckets public, apply an SCP deny at the OU level. A frequent error is misusing SCPs for day-to-day permissions—they are blunt instruments and can block automation if misapplied. Closing question: for a single resource shared with one external account, which policy type should you prefer and why? The resource policy is best because it provides explicit resource-scoped sharing without creating cross-account identities.

First, identity-based policies attach to principals and declare what those identities may do; test them with the policy simulator and prefer role attachments over long-lived users. Second, resource-based policies live on the resource and are the right tool for cross-account sharing—always scope principals and use conditions like PrincipalOrgID where appropriate. Third, Service Control Policies provide organization-level guardrails by limiting the maximum permissions in accounts; they do not grant permissions and must be used sparingly and tested carefully. Keep in mind the policy evaluation rule: an action is allowed only if SCPs permit it and both identity and resource policies allow it without explicit deny.
